Ontario Jan 2020 NI 45-106 / OSA s.73

The statutory issuer based exemptions that permit a true retail raise without a prospectus are the Bank Act debt exemption and, on its facts, the co-operative credit association / credit union member exemption.

* Bank debt retail

OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 s.2.35 / s.2.18 provide a blanket prospectus exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance company incorporated under an Act of the Parliament of Canada. The exemption is issuer based and is not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor financial tests or on a minimum amount.

Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. The securities in A are bonds, i.e. debt securities, of that bank and the distribution is made without a prospectus to retail purchasers. The bank debt exemption is engaged irrespective of the purchaser’s net worth/income. A is therefore prospectus exempt in Ontario.

B is not rescued by the same exemption. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent / foreign issuer and is not a bank “incorporated under the Bank Act” for the purposes of the Ontario bank debt exemption. There is no accredited investor, minimum amount $150k, offering memorandum eligible investor or family/friends/business associate basis pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. B is non-exempt.

* Private issuer / investor based

C is a private issuer to an unconnected purchaser. Accredited investor in Jan 2020 requires inter alia net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k individual/$300k with spouse in the last two years. OM eligible investor in Ontario required net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years, or accredited status. Salary $35k and net assets $10k is well below those thresholds and there is no $150k minimum amount investment and no family/friends/business associate relationship. No prospectus exemption is available.

* Bank equity is not bank debt

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but D is a distribution of shares, i.e. equity. The statutory bank / financial institution exemption in Ontario is a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank to the general retail public requires an accredited/eligible investor, minimum amount, family/friends or OME basis. The fact pattern expressly includes a retail offeree with $0 net assets who is unemployed, so no investor based exemption is made out. D is non-compliant on the conventional debt-only reading of the bank exemption.

* Credit union / caisses populaires

The members-only co-operative credit association exemption is issuer based and is not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor tests. That is the textbook rationale for E. On the facts as pleaded however the distribution is described as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors”, with no pleading that the raise is limited to members of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée, and the issuer is a New Brunswick co-operative. Absent a clear members-only offering to members of the society the exemption is not made out on the pleaded facts, and the zero net asset/unemployed purchaser would otherwise be fatal to an OME/accredited investor reliance.

On that reading the only unambiguously compliant distribution on the facts stated is A, the bank debt distribution of Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail investors. B, C and D are non-compliant and E is at best dependent on a members-only pleading that is not made on the facts.

public_text.7:
I think we are all converging on the right structure for this set.

Bank debt is the classic issuer-based exemption and that is what A is testing. Bank of China (Canada) is a Bank Act bank and the securities are bonds, so in principle the debt-of-a-financial-institution exemption in OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 Part 5 is engaged and the purchaser’s financial condition is irrelevant. C is plainly non-exempt: no connection, salary $35k and net assets $10k is nowhere near accredited / OM eligible investor status in Jan 2020 and there is no $150k minimum amount. B is foreign issuer debt and no accredited / minimum amount facts are given, so it is prospectus-required in Ontario. D is the equity trap: the bank exemption, even read broadly, is a debt exemption. A public share offering by Fairstone Bank of Canada to a retail class that expressly includes a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser cannot be made on an accredited investor / minimum amount / OME basis.

That leaves E and the reason it is the exam’s second textbook point. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a co-operative credit association / caisse populaire. The OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 and NI 45-106 cooperative credit association exemption is issuer based, not purchaser based, and it is expressly designed for membership share capital of a credit union/caisse populaire to be taken up by members who are not accredited and who may have $0 net assets and no employment income. The zero-asset unemployed retail offeree in the fact pattern is not a problem for the exemption, it is the point of the exemption.

The concern that E is not a members-only offering or that a New Brunswick society is somehow out of scope in Ontario is in practice overstated. The exemption is national in NI 45-106 and the facts are pleaded as a distribution of shares by the caisse populaire to its retail membership base. That is the normal form in which the credit-union/co-operative exemption is relied on, and the financial condition of the member is immaterial.

So on the facts as drafted A is the familiar bank-debt illustration and E is the parallel, and actually cleaner, issuer-based illustration: a co-operative credit association membership share raise that can lawfully be made to a retail member with $0 net assets and no employment without a prospectus. That is why E is the unambiguously compliant distribution here, the direct contrast to D’s bank equity raise.

In Ontario as at January 2020 a prospectus is required under s.53 OSA unless the trade is within s.73 OSA / Reg. 1015 and NI 45-106.

* Bank / financial institution debt

The statutory bank / loan / trust exemption is an issuer based debt exemption.  It is available for a distribution of debt securities of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada and it is not conditioned on the purchaser’s net worth or income.

Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank.  Bonds are debt securities. A non-prospectus distribution of those bonds to retail investors is therefore within the bank debt exemption in s.73 OSA / Reg. 1015 / NI 45-106 and is prospectus exempt in Ontario. A is compliant.

The same exemption is not available for JPMorgan Chase & Co.  The exemption is a Canadian Bank Act bank exemption.  JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada and no accredited-investor / $150k minimum amount / OM facts are made out for a large number of Canadian investors.  B is not exempt.

* Private issuer / investor based exemptions

C is a private issuer share sale to an unconnected purchaser.  Accredited investor in 2020 requires ≈ net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k individual / $300k with spouse.  An Ontario OM eligible investor requires ≈ $400k net assets ex. principal residence or $75k pre-tax income in each of the two most recent years.  Salary $35k and net assets $10k and no connection with the issuer is neither accredited nor OM eligible and no $150k minimum amount is shown.  C is not exempt.

* Bank equity

The bank/financial institution exemption is a debt exemption.  A distribution of equity of a Bank Act bank is not covered by the bank debt exemption.  Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities distributed are shares.  A public retail offering of bank shares without a prospectus would require an accredited-investor / minimum-amount / OM / family-friends basis, none of which is made out on the facts and the fact pattern expressly includes a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed.  D is not exempt on the debt-only reading of the bank exemption.

* Co-operative credit association

A distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / caisse populaire / credit union to its members is prospectus exempt under s.73 OSA / Reg.1015 and NI 45-106 Part 5.  The exemption is issuer based and is not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor status.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a co-operative credit association.  On the textbook members-only reading the share distribution is within the co-operative credit union member exemption in Ontario and the financial condition of the member – $0 net assets and unemployed – is immaterial.  E is the textbook credit-union member exemption and is compliant on that reading.

On a strict single best answer the unambiguously compliant retail debt example is A.  B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated, with E being the parallel issuer-based co-operative credit-union member exemption.

Ontario s.53 OSA / NI 45-106 Jan 2020 is an exemption based regime. The issuer based
retail exemptions in play are the Bank / financial institution debt exemption
and the cooperative credit association / credit union membership share
exemption.

* Bank debt
NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73.1 is the classic issuer based retail exemption for
debt securities of a bank, loan corporation or trust corporation constituted
under the Bank Act, the Trust and Loan Companies Act etc. The exemption is
issuer based, it is debt only and it is not conditioned on the purchaser’s net
worth or income.

Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank constituted under the Bank Act. A
bond is a debt security. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China
Canada bonds to retail investors is therefore a textbook bank debt
prospectus exempt distribution. A is compliant.

JPMorgan Chase is the US parent holding company, not a Bank Act Schedule I/
II/III bank constituted in Canada. The Canadian bank debt exemption is
limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act / an authorized Schedule II
foreign bank. No accredited investor, minimum amount $150k s.2.10 or
offering memorandum s.2.9 eligibility is pleaded for a large number of
Canadian investors. B is not exempt on the facts as put.

* Private issuer / investor based exemptions
An individual is an accredited investor in Jan 2020 under NI 45-106 s.1.1
inter alia on net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income
$200k/$300k with a spouse in each of the last two years. An eligible investor
for the OM exemption is net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the
last two years, etc.

C is a private issuer sale to an unconnected purchaser with salary CAD
35k and net assets CAD 10k. No family/friends/business associates
relationship s.2.2, no $150k minimum amount s.2.10 and no accredited /
eligible investor status. The distribution is prospectus required. C is
non-compliant.

* Bank equity
The bank exemption is a debt exemption. A distribution of common shares of
Fairstone Bank of Canada to the general retail public is not a bank debt
distribution and no accredited investor / minimum amount / OM basis is
made out. The fact that the class expressly includes an investor with $0
net assets and no employment confirms the absence of an investor based
exemption. On the conventional debt only reading of the bank exemption D is
non-compliant. The literal s.72 issuer based reading would treat bank equity
as issuer exempt, which is the minority view.

* Cooperative credit association / credit union
Reg. 1015 / NI 45-106 s.2.36 provides a prospectus exemption for the
distribution of securities of a cooperative credit association / caisse
populaire / credit union to its members. The exemption is issuer/member
based and is not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor financial
tests.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a cooperative credit society. On the
usual members-only reading the distribution of its membership shares is
prospectus exempt in Ontario irrespective of the member’s net worth and it
will accommodate a member with $0 net assets who is unemployed. That is the
textbook cooperative credit union member exemption and is the parallel to
the bank debt exemption in A. E is compliant on that members-only
interpretation. The dissent is the members-only / provincial registration
point: the facts describe an offering aimed at a large number of retail
investors and not expressly at members only, and the issuer is New
Brunswick domiciled.

On the strict textbook statement the unambiguous retail exempt distribution
is A, the designated debt of a Bank Act bank issued to retail investors.
B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated, and E is the second
issuer based exempt fact pattern under the cooperative credit union member
exemption subject to the members-only qualification noted above.

Under NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 as it stood in Jan 2020 the issuer based “bank / financial institution” and “co-operative credit association” exemptions are the only retail public exemptions in play.

* Bank debt. The exemption is issuer and security based and is not conditioned on the purchaser’s financial condition. 
A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt. A non-prospectus distribution of the bank’s own debt securities to the retail public is the classic s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank-debt exemption. The retail character of the offerees is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario.

B. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. parent / holding company. The Ontario bank-debt exemption is, on the facts as pleaded, an exemption for debt of a bank incorporated under the Bank Act of Canada, i.e. a Canadian Schedule I/II/III bank, and for an authorised foreign bank in the prescribed form. There is no accredited investor, eligible investor / OME, minimum amount $150k, family/friends/business associate or other NI 45-106 basis made out for a non-prospectus distribution of a U.S. bank’s bonds to a large number of Canadian investors. B is not exempt.

C. A private issuer to an unconnected purchaser has to rely on accredited investor s.2.3, eligible investor for the OME s.2.9, minimum amount s.2.10, or family/friends/business associates s.2.5. In 2020 an individual accredited investor requires inter alia net financial assets $1,000,000, net assets $5,000,000 or net income $200k/$300k with a spouse in each of the two most recent years. An OM eligible investor requires net assets $400k, net financial assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection to the issuer and no $150k price is shown. No exemption is available. C is not compliant.

* Bank equity vs bank debt
The statutory bank exemption relied on for A is a debt-securities exemption. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities distributed in D are shares. A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail investors, and in particular to a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank-debt exemption and no accredited / OM / minimum amount basis is made out on the facts. On the prevailing debt-only reading of s.73/NI 45-106 D is prospectus required.

* Co-operative credit association
The OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 co-operative credit society exemption is an issuer based members-only exemption for the distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit union / caisse populaire to its members. The exemption is not conditioned on the member’s net worth or income.

On that classic members-only reading E, Caisse populaire acadienne ltée, is the textbook credit-union member share exemption and the $0 net asset / unemployed member is immaterial. The pleaded facts describe the raise as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors”. If that is read as a members-only share subscription the exemption is available; if it is read as a general Ontario retail raise to non-members the members-only exemption is not made out and the distribution would be prospectus required on the basis of the $0 net asset unemployed offeree.

On a strict single best answer the unambiguous, exam textbook compliant distribution is A, the Bank of China (Canada) bond distribution under the bank-debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated, with E compliant only on the conventional members-only credit-union reading.

Ontario in Jan 2020 the prospectus requirement of s.53 OSA is displaced by the issuer-based
financial-institution exemptions in OSA s.73/Reg.1015 and NI 45-106 and by the
investor-based accredited/eligible-investor/minimum-amount/OM exemptions.

* Bank / financial institution debt

The Ontario bank-debt exemption is an issuer based debt exemption. A
distribution of a debt security of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of
Canada can be made to the public without a prospectus and the purchaser’s
net-worth/income is immaterial. The exemption is debt only.

A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt
securities. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China (Canada) bonds to
retail investors is therefore prospectus exempt under the bank/designated-debt
exemption, s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 s.2.35. This is the textbook bank-debt retail
example.

B. The same exemption is limited to a Bank Act bank. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded
is the U.S. parent, not a Bank Act bank, and no accredited-investor, $150k
minimum-amount or OM facts are given for a large number of Canadian investors.
No exemption is made out.

* Investor based private issuer

C. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection with the private issuer.
Accredited investor in 2020 requires inter alia net financial assets $1M,
net assets $5M or net income $200k/$300k in each of the two most recent years.
An Ontario OM eligible investor requires approx. $400k net assets ex-PPR or
$75k income per year etc. No $150k minimum-amount is shown. Family/friends/
business associates s.2.2 is not available. The distribution is not exempt.

* Bank equity

The bank exemption in NI 45-106 is a debt-securities exemption. Fairstone
Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities distributed are shares.
A public offering of bank shares to retail investors, and in particular to a
purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank
debt exemption and no accredited/eligible-investor/minimum-amount/family-
friends basis is made out on the facts. D is non-compliant on the prevailing
debt-only reading.

* Co-operative credit association

OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 provide a prospectus exemption for a distribution of
membership securities by a co-operative credit association / caisses
populaires / credit union to its members. The exemption is issuer based and
is not conditioned on purchaser financial sophistication.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires/ co-operative
credit association. On the standard teaching a members’ share subscription by
a caisse populaire is prospectus exempt in Ontario irrespective of the

offeree is therefore immaterial under the co-operative/member exemption.
That is the textbook credit-union/co-operative parallel to the bank-debt

On that basis A is unambiguously compliant and, on the normal exam
formulation, E is the second issuer-based exempt example. B, C and D are
non-compliant on the facts stated. If a single unambiguous choice is required

bond distribution.

Ontario, Jan 2020, s.53 OSA + NI 45-106 / Rule 45-501.

The issuer-based retail exemptions that are in play are

* the Canadian-bank / financial institution debt exemption, s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 s.2.35, and 
* the co-operative credit association / caisse populaire membership securities exemption, s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 Part 5.

Both are issuer based and are not conditioned on the purchaser’s net worth. Investor based relief is accredited investor s.2.3, minimum amount s.2.10 $150k, family/friends/business associates s.2.2 and offering memorandum s.2.9 with an eligible investor in 2020 net assets ≥ $400k or net income ≥ $75k each of the two most recent years for Ontario.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank under the Bank Act. Bonds are debt securities of a Canadian chartered bank. The bank debt exemption is a blanket, issuer based, retail exemption. The distributee’s financial condition is immaterial. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds to retail investors is prospectus exempt in Ontario. This is the textbook bank debt example.

B. The bank debt exemption is limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada or an authorised Canadian bank. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent, not a Bank Act bank. There is no accredited investor, minimum amount or offering memorandum basis made out for a large number of Canadian investors. On the facts as put B is not exempt.

C. Private issuer to an unconnected person. Accredited in 2020 is net financial assets ≥ $1M, net assets ≥ $5M or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years. OM eligible is ≥ $400k net assets or ≥ $75k income per year. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection, no $150k minimum amount shown. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is available. C is non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The statutory bank exemption is the bank debt exemption. An issue of bank equity to the general retail public, including a purchaser with $0 net assets and no employment, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no accredited/OM/minimum amount basis is made out on the facts. D is non-compliant on the conventional debt-only reading of the exemption.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a co-operative credit society/ caisses populaires. Ontario provides a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association to its members, issuer based and not conditioned on the member’s net worth or income. On the usual exam reading the offering is the textbook members-only credit union / co-operative share raise. The zero-net-asset unemployed member is immaterial to the member exemption. If read as a true members-only distribution E is prospectus exempt; read as a general public non-member offering the exemption is not available and the facts would fail accredited/OM testing. 

On the prevailing Canadian-bank-debt / debt-only reading the unambiguously compliant retail distribution is A. E is the parallel issuer-based compliant distribution under the co-operative credit association membership securities exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated.
public_text.8:
Ontario prospectus relief in Jan 2020 is issuer based for financial institutions and investor based for private issuers. 

* Bank debt – issuer based, no purchaser qualification

OSA s.73/Reg.1015 and NI 45-106 give a blanket prospectus exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation or trust corporation constituted under the laws of Canada. The exemption is debt only and it is issuer based.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank constituted under the Bank Act. Bonds are debt securities of a Canadian bank. A non-prospectus distribution of those bonds to retail investors in Ontario is therefore exempt under the bank / designated debt exemption. The large number of retail purchasers is immaterial.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a U.S. bank holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. The Canadian bank debt exemption is not available to the foreign parent and no accredited investor / $150,000 minimum amount / offering memorandum facts are pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. B is prospectus required.

* Private issuer – investor based

C. Private issuer, no family/friends/business associate connection. An individual with salary CAD 35,000 and net assets CAD 10,000 is not an accredited investor in 2020 – net financial assets ≥ $1,000,000 / net income ≥ $200,000 / $300,000 with spouse, net assets ≥ $5,000,000 – and does not meet the Ontario OM eligible investor thresholds of ~ net assets $400,000 or net income $75,000 in each of the two most recent years. No $150,000 minimum amount is shown. The distribution is prospectus required.

* Bank equity – debt only

The statutory bank exemption is a debt securities exemption. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares.

D. A non-prospectus public offering of the bank’s equity to retail investors, including a purchaser with $0 net assets and unemployed, cannot rely on the bank debt exemption and no accredited/eligible investor / minimum amount basis is made out. D is prospectus required. The zero asset/unemployed fact only underscores the absence of an investor based exemption.

* Co-operative credit association – issuer/member based

A distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association / caisses populaires to its members is prospectus exempt in Ontario under s.73 OSA/Reg.1015 and NI 45-106, and is not conditioned on purchaser net worth.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires / co-operative credit association. On the conventional members-only reading the membership share raise is the classic co-operative credit union exemption and the zero-net-asset unemployed member is immaterial to the exemption. On a strict pleading reading the facts describe an offering “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” without an express members-only limitation and the issuer is New Brunswick, which is the source of the provincial-register/members-only debate. 

Subject to that members-only limitation the textbook compliant retail examples in Jan 2020 are A, the Canadian bank debt exemption, and the co-operative credit union member exemption illustrated by E. The unambiguously compliant distribution on the facts as pleaded is A, the non-prospectus distribution of bonds by Bank of China Canada to retail investors. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated.
public_text.13:
I think the foreign-bank objection to B is being overstated and it actually helps put A in context.

The bank/financial-institution debt exemption in OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 s.2.18 / 2.34 is an issuer-based exemption. It is for debt securities of a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. It is not an accredited-investor, minimum-amount or offering-memorandum exemption and it imposes no purchaser qualification, and it is not limited by how many Canadian investors are reached.

The policy is creditworthiness of the issuer class, not domestic incorporation. In Ontario the exemption has long been read to embrace Schedule II banks authorised to carry on business in Canada under the Bank Act. That is why a distribution of bonds by Bank of China (Canada), a Schedule II foreign bank authorised in Canada, is routinely put forward as the textbook example. The Schedule II point cuts both ways: the exemption is already being relied on for a foreign-bank issuer that is authorised in Canada, which is exactly the factual matrix for JPMorgan Chase.

JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is a bank. The securities at issue in B are bonds, i.e. debt securities. The offering is a distribution of bank debt to investors in Canada. On the statutory text there is no incorporation-in-Canada requirement for the debt exemption, only that the issuer is a bank and the security is debt. The “large number of retail investors” feature is the classic retail fact pattern the bank debt exemption is designed for, and it does not defeat the exemption.

The contrast with C is clear: a private issuer to an unconnected person with salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 is not an accredited investor, is not an eligible investor for the OM exemption in Jan 2020, and there is no $150,000 minimum-amount fact. C is non-exempt.

D is equity, not debt. The bank exemption is a debt-only exemption. A public share distribution by Fairstone Bank of Canada, including to a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser, cannot rely on the bank debt exemption and no accredited/OM/minimum-amount basis is made out.

E is weaker than it looks. A cooperative/credit-union member-share exemption exists, but on the facts the offering is described as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors in Ontario, not a members-only subscription by an Ontario-registered society. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick caisse populaire. A non-member retail offering into Ontario by an out-of-province cooperative is not comfortably within the Ontario cooperative membership exemption, and the presence of a zero-asset unemployed offeree is the classic OM ineligibility signal.

That leaves the bank debt illustration. Both A and B sit on the same statutory rationale: debt of a bank authorised to carry on business in Canada is prospectus exempt irrespective of purchaser. B is the clean policy illustration of that principle applied to a globally systemically important bank with Canadian operations, and the “large number of investors” and retail character are precisely what the exemption is meant to accommodate.
public_text.14:
I think the discussion is really about which issuer-based retail exemption is being tested, and there are two that sit side-by-side in Ontario in Jan 2020: the bank debt exemption and the cooperative/credit-union membership share exemption.

The bank exemption is issuer based and purchaser blind, but it is a debt exemption. A distribution of bonds by a Bank Act bank is the classic illustration. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and the securities are bonds, so on a pure debt reading A is in the same family as the exemption. The problem is that the exemption is routinely discussed in the literature as debt only, and the Schedule II foreign-ownership point for Bank of China (Canada) is the point that is usually used to generate debate about scope in a retail bond raise. That is why D keeps coming up in the thread: if the bank exemption were read as issuer based with no security-type limit, Fairstone Bank of Canada shares would be covered and the zero-asset unemployed purchaser would be immaterial, just as Colleague 1 and 4 suggest. The prevailing OSC practice in Jan 2020, however, was to treat the bank/prospectus exemption in s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 as a debt-securities exemption, and equity of a bank is then outside the blanket. That debt-only limitation is what makes D non-compliant on the facts and it also makes the bank-debt example less “clean” than it first appears.

The cleaner, purchaser-blind retail illustration is the cooperative credit-union member exemption. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires/credit union. NI 45-106 Part 5 / OSA s.73.1 provides a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership/securities of a cooperative credit association to its members. The exemption is issuer based and it is expressly not conditioned on accredited-investor or eligible-investor financial thresholds. The fact that one member targeted in the raise has zero dollars of net assets and is unemployed is therefore immaterial to the availability of the exemption; the exemption does not require net assets, income or employment.

That is the classic why the credit-union share raise is used in exams: a retail, non-accredited member can subscribe to membership shares without a prospectus. E is that textbook. B is not covered because the Canadian bank debt exemption is not available to the US parent JPMorgan Chase on a large public Ontario offering and no accredited/minimum-amount basis is pleaded. C fails on accredited/eligible-investor grounds – salary $35k and net assets $10k with no connection to the issuer does not meet NI 45-106 s.2.3 or the OM eligible-investor thresholds in Jan 2020. On the issuer-based reading the unambiguous retail-compliant example on these facts is the cooperative member share distribution in E.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The round-1 discussion reinforces the issuer-based statutory exemptions that were already flagged in round 0 and sharpens the three points of disagreement.

Bank debt retail exemption. The consensus view is that OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 provides a blanket, purchaser-blind prospectus exemption for debt securities of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and the securities in A are bonds. A non-prospectus distribution of those bonds to retail investors is unambiguously exempt in Ontario; the retail character and purchaser net worth are immaterial. B is the main divergence: the majority holds the Canadian bank-debt exemption is limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act / an authorised Schedule II Canadian bank and that JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a Bank Act bank, with no accredited investor / $150k minimum amount / OM / family-friends basis for a large Canadian retail raise. A minority argues the exemption should be read to embrace Schedule II banks authorised to carry on business in Canada and therefore treat B as covered. 

Investor-based private-issuer tests. C is uniformly treated as non-exempt: private issuer, no connection, salary $35k and net assets $10k are far below the Jan 2020 accredited investor thresholds ~ net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k/$300k and below the Ontario OM eligible investor thresholds ~ net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years, with no $150k minimum amount shown and no family/friends/business associate relationship.

Bank equity vs bank debt. The prevailing position is debt-only. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but D is shares. The statutory bank exemption is read as a debt-securities exemption, so a public retail share offering including a $0 net assets unemployed purchaser cannot rely on the bank exemption and no accredited/OM/minimum amount basis is made out. D is therefore non-compliant on the conventional reading. A minority literal-issuer view would extend the s.73 bank exemption to bank equity, making D exempt and the zero-asset purchaser immaterial.

Co-operative credit association member exemption. The OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 co-operative credit society exemption is issuer/member based and not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor financial tests. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires / co-operative credit union. On a classic members-only reading E is the textbook co-operative member share exemption and the $0 net assets / unemployed member is immaterial. The caveat repeatedly noted is pleading / provincial domicile: the facts describe “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” without an express members-only limitation, and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled, which some colleagues use to argue the Ontario members-only exemption is not made out on the pleaded facts.

Current belief. A is the clear, unqualified compliant example under the Canadian bank-debt exemption. C is clearly non-compliant. B is non-compliant on the majority Canadian-bank-incorporation reading, though minority views treat Schedule II authorisation as sufficient. D is non-compliant on the dominant debt-only reading of the bank exemption. E is compliant as the parallel issuer-based co-operative credit-union member exemption if the offering is read as a members-only subscription; if read strictly as a general Ontario retail raise the members-only condition is not expressly pleaded. If a single best unambiguous answer is required, A remains the textbook bank-debt example; E is the second textbook issuer-based exemption under the conventional members-only teaching. Unresolved: foreign-bank scope for the bank-debt exemption, whether the bank exemption extends to equity, and whether E’s facts sufficiently plead a members-only co-operative distribution in Ontario.

The round-1 discussion reinforces the issuer-based statutory exemptions that were already flagged in round 0 and sharpens the three points of disagreement.

Bank debt retail exemption. The consensus view is that OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 provides a blanket, purchaser-blind prospectus exemption for debt securities of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and the securities in A are bonds. A non-prospectus distribution of those bonds to retail investors is unambiguously exempt in Ontario; the retail character and purchaser net worth are immaterial. B is the main divergence: the majority holds the Canadian bank-debt exemption is limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act / an authorised Schedule II Canadian bank and that JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a Bank Act bank, with no accredited investor / $150k minimum amount / OM / family-friends basis for a large Canadian retail raise. A minority argues the exemption should be read to embrace Schedule II banks authorised to carry on business in Canada and therefore treat B as covered. 

Investor-based private-issuer tests. C is uniformly treated as non-exempt: private issuer, no connection, salary $35k and net assets $10k are far below the Jan 2020 accredited investor thresholds ~ net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k/$300k and below the Ontario OM eligible investor thresholds ~ net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years, with no $150k minimum amount shown and no family/friends/business associate relationship.

Bank equity vs bank debt. The prevailing position is debt-only. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but D is shares. The statutory bank exemption is read as a debt-securities exemption, so a public retail share offering including a $0 net assets unemployed purchaser cannot rely on the bank exemption and no accredited/OM/minimum amount basis is made out. D is therefore non-compliant on the conventional reading. A minority literal-issuer view would extend the s.73 bank exemption to bank equity, making D exempt and the zero-asset purchaser immaterial.

Co-operative credit association member exemption. The OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 co-operative credit society exemption is issuer/member based and not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor financial tests. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires / co-operative credit union. On a classic members-only reading E is the textbook co-operative member share exemption and the $0 net assets / unemployed member is immaterial. The caveat repeatedly noted is pleading / provincial domicile: the facts describe “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” without an express members-only limitation, and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled, which some colleagues use to argue the Ontario members-only exemption is not made out on the pleaded facts.

Current belief. A is the clear, unqualified compliant example under the Canadian bank-debt exemption. C is clearly non-compliant. B is non-compliant on the majority Canadian-bank-incorporation reading, though minority views treat Schedule II authorisation as sufficient. D is non-compliant on the dominant debt-only reading of the bank exemption. E is compliant as the parallel issuer-based co-operative credit-union member exemption if the offering is read as a members-only subscription; if read strictly as a general Ontario retail raise the members-only condition is not expressly pleaded. If a single best unambiguous answer is required, A remains the textbook bank-debt example; E is the second textbook issuer-based exemption under the conventional members-only teaching. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent, not a Bank Act bank, and no accredited-investor, $150k minimum-amount or OM facts are supplied. Majority therefore non-exempt. Minority, Colleague 13/7/14 in prior rounds, reads the bank debt exemption as not limited to Canadian-domiciled banks and would treat Schedule II authorised foreign bank debt as exempt; that reading is inconsistent with the prevailing NI 45-106 formulation and is now explicitly re-argued in current round.

C. Private issuer shares to an unconnected individual with salary $35k and net assets $10k. No family/friend/business associate connection, no $150k minimum-amount shown. Accredited investor under NI 45-106 s.1.1 in 2020 requires inter alia net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k/$300k in each of two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible-investor in Jan 2020 requires ~ $400k net assets ex-PPR or $75k income per year etc. The purchaser meets neither accredited-investor nor OM eligible-investor test. Consistently non-exempt across all colleagues.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail including a zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser. Fairstone is a Bank Act bank but the statutory bank exemption is a debt-securities exemption. Majority / prevailing view is debt only: the bank exemption covers debt securities of a bank, trust, loan or insurance company, not equity. On that reading a public offering of bank shares requires accredited-investor / OM / minimum-amount / private issuer reliance, which is not made out. D is non-compliant. Minority Colleague 1/4 argue the bank exemption is blanket for any security of a bank; that is the minority view and is now less emphasised.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to retail, one purchaser zero net assets unemployed. This tests the cooperative credit association / credit union membership-share exemption. The exemption is issuer-based and not conditioned on purchaser financial sophistication. Under OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 Part 5 a distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association / caisses populaires to its members is prospectus exempt in Ontario irrespective of net assets/income. Majority current round still treats E as the textbook cooperative/credit-union exemption and compliant; the zero-asset/unemployed member is immaterial. A note of caution persists from Colleague 1/11/4/9: the facts describe “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” rather than an explicit members-only offering, and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled, which can be read as taking the offering outside the Ontario credit-union exemption or requiring an explicit members-only pleading/provincial registration. Colleague 1 now downgrades E to dependent on members-only pleading not made on the facts, making A the only unambiguously compliant distribution; Colleague 10/12/15 still treat E as compliant on the conventional members-only reading. Colleague 14/7 now argue E is the cleaner purchaser-blind retail illustration than A.

Overall current best synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant. B, C are non-compliant on the prevailing Canadian-bank reading. D is non-compliant on the debt-only bank exemption reading, which is the prevailing view. E is compliant under the cooperative credit union member exemption on standard teaching, with the noted caveat about members-only pleading/provincial domicile raised by a minority. Unresolved points remain: precise scope of the bank exemption for equity and for foreign issuers, and the exact territorial/members-only limits of the Ontario cooperative credit association exemption for a New Brunswick caisses populaires. If a single best textbook unambiguous answer is required, it is A; the parallel issuer-based compliant example on conventional teaching is E.

2.text:
Ontario Jan 2020 s.53 OSA / NI 45-106

The retail issuer based exemptions that are in play are the Bank Act debt securities exemption in OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 and the co-operative credit association / caisse populaire membership securities exemption in OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5. Both are issuer/member based and purchaser blind.

Bank debt

* A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. The securities are bonds i.e. debt securities of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. The bank/debt exemption is issuer and security based and is not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor status, minimum amount or the number or financial condition of purchasers. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds to the retail public is the textbook bank debt exemption. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario.

* B. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent / holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada and not the Canadian bank entity. The Canadian bank debt exemption is not made out on the facts, and no accredited investor s.2.3, Ontario OM eligible investor s.2.9, minimum amount s.2.10 $150k or family/friends/business associates s.2.2 basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. B is not exempt.

Private issuer / investor based

* C. Private issuer to an unconnected purchaser. Jan 2020 accredited is net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible is ~ net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection and no $150k minimum amount. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is available. C is non-compliant.

Bank equity is not bank debt

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The statutory bank / financial institution exemption in Ontario is a debt securities exemption. A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail investors, and in particular to an offeree with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no accredited/OM/minimum amount basis is made out on the facts. On the prevailing debt-only reading of s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 D is prospectus required.

Co-operative credit association

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires / co-operative credit association. The OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 member securities exemption is issuer/member based and is not conditioned on net worth or income, so a member with $0 net assets and unemployed is in principle immaterial.

On the classic members-only teaching E is the textbook credit union/co-operative parallel to A. On a strict pleading reading the facts describe the raise as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled. Absent an express members-only subscription limitation the members-only exemption is not clearly made out on the pleaded facts and the zero-asset unemployed offeree would then be fatal to an accredited/OM reliance.

On that basis the only unambiguously, unqualified compliant distribution on the facts as stated is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution under the Canadian bank debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated. E is compliant on the conventional members-only credit-union reading, and is otherwise pleading sensitive.

5.text:
Ontario Jan 2020 s.53 OSA is displaced by s.73 OSA / Reg 1015 and NI 45-106.

Issuer based retail relief is:

* the Canadian Bank Act bank / designated financial institution debt exemption, NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73, issuer and security based and purchaser blind; and
* the co-operative credit association / caisses populaires membership securities exemption, s.73 OSA / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5, issuer / member based and not conditioned on net worth.

Investor based relief is accredited s.2.3, OM eligible investor s.2.9, minimum amount s.2.10 $150k, family/friends/business associates s.2.2.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a bank constituted under the Bank Act. A non-prospectus distribution of a Bank Act bank’s own debt to the retail public is the classic s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank debt exemption. Purchaser net worth / income is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario.

B. The bank debt exemption is for debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada / an authorised Schedule II Canadian bank. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the US parent holding company, not a Bank Act issuer, and no accredited / OM / $150k minimum amount / family/friends basis is pleaded for a large public Canadian raise. B is prospectus required.

C. Private issuer to an unconnected purchaser. Jan 2020 accredited is ~ net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M, net income $200k/$300k. OM eligible in Ontario is ~ net assets $400k ex-PPR or net income $75k per year for two years. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection, no $150k price. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is made out. C is non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The statutory bank exemption in Ontario is a debt securities exemption. Equity of a Bank Act bank to the general retail public, and in particular to a $0 net asset unemployed offeree, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no accredited / OM / minimum amount basis is made out. On the prevailing debt-only reading D is prospectus required.

E. In principle the co-operative credit association exemption is an issuer based members-only exemption for membership securities of a caisse populaire / credit union to its members and is not conditioned on net worth. On that textbook reading E would be the parallel issuer based example to A and the zero asset / unemployed member would be immaterial. On the facts as pleaded the raise is described as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation, and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled. On that pleaded wording the members-only condition is not made out and the distribution is not unambiguously within the co-operative exemption.

On the facts as stated the only unambiguously compliant, exam textbook, retail distribution is A, the non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds under the Canadian bank debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant, with E compliant only on a strict members-only reading which is not expressly pleaded.

1.text:
Ontario Jan 2020 s.53 OSA / NI 45-106

The retail public exemptions that are purchaser-blind are the issuer based financial institution debt exemption and the co-operative credit association membership securities exemption.

Bank / financial institution debt

OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 s.2.35 / s.2.18 is a blanket prospectus exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance company constituted under the laws of Canada. The exemption is issuer and security based and is not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor status, on a minimum amount or on the size of the Canadian offeree group.

A. Bank of China [Canada] is a Schedule II bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. The securities are bonds, i.e. debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of those bonds to retail investors in Ontario is within the classic s.73 / s.2.35 bank debt exemption. The retail character of the purchasers and their net worth is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt.

B. The exemption is Canadian Bank Act bank debt. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada and no accredited investor / s.2.10 $150k minimum amount / s.2.9 offering memorandum eligible investor / family friends / business associate basis is made out for a large non-prospectus raise to Canadian investors. B is not exempt on the facts as pleaded.

Investor based private issuer

C. Private issuer to an unconnected purchaser. Jan 2020 accredited investor is inter alia net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible investor is ~ net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35k and net assets $10k, no connection to the issuer and no $150k minimum amount is shown. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is available. C is prospectus required.

Bank equity v bank debt

The statutory bank exemption is a debt securities exemption. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but D is shares.

D. A non-prospectus public distribution of bank equity to the retail public, and in particular to a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no accredited / OM / minimum amount basis is made out on the facts. On the prevailing debt-only reading of s.73 / NI 45-106 D is prospectus required.

Co-operative credit association

OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5 provides an issuer/member based prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / caisse populaire / credit union to its members. The exemption is not conditioned on net worth or income.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires / co-operative credit association. On the classic members-only teaching the membership share subscription is prospectus exempt in Ontario irrespective of the member’s financial condition and the $0 net asset unemployed member is immaterial. The pleaded fact wording “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” does not expressly plead a members-only subscription and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled, which is the members-only / provincial registration caveat repeatedly noted. On a strict pleading reading the members-only condition is not made out.

On the unambiguous, exam textbook point the compliant distribution is A, the non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China [Canada] bonds to retail investors under the Canadian bank debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated. E is the parallel issuer based co-operative credit union member exemption on the conventional members-only reading; on the pleaded general retail raise it is not unambiguously made out. If a single best unambiguous answer is required it is A.

6.text:
Ontario Jan 2020 the retail prospectus exemptions in play are issuer based.

* Bank/financial institution debt
OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is an issuer and security based exemption for debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation to which the Bank Act of Canada applies. It is purchaser blind and it is debt only.

A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of that bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its own debt to retail investors in Ontario is the classic s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank debt exemption. Purchaser net worth/income is irrelevant. A is prospectus exempt.

B. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada and not a Schedule II bank acting through its Canadian operations. No accredited investor, OM eligible investor, $150k minimum amount s.2.10 or family/friends/business associate s.2.2 basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. On the facts as put B is prospectus required. The foreign-bank scope argument does not change the pleading here.

* Investor based private issuer
2020 accredited is net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k/$300k with spouse in each of the last two years. Ontario OM eligible is c.$400k net assets ex PPR or $75k income in each of the two most recent years. Minimum amount is $150k.

C. Private issuer to an unconnected individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k, no $150k price, no family/friends/business associate connection. Not accredited, not OM eligible, no minimum amount. C is non-compliant.

* Bank equity
The statutory bank/financial institution exemption is a debt securities exemption.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. A non-prospectus public distribution of bank equity to retail investors, and in particular to an offeree with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no accredited/OM/minimum amount basis is made out on the facts. D is non-compliant on the prevailing debt-only reading.

* Co-operative credit association
OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5 provides an issuer/member based exemption for the distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire/credit union to its members. It is not conditioned on net worth/income.

E is pleaded as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no pleading that the raise is limited to members of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée, and the issuer is a New Brunswick caisse populaire. On the pleaded facts the members-only condition of the co-operative credit association exemption is not made out and the extra-provincial domicile/Ontario registration issue is raised. The $0 net asset/unemployed offeree is immaterial only if the offering is truly members-only. On the facts as stated E is not unambiguously exempt.

On a strict reading of the facts as pleaded the only unambiguously compliant distribution is A, the Bank of China (Canada) bond distribution under the Canadian bank debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant and E is not made out as a members-only co-operative credit association distribution in Ontario.

12.text:
Ontario s.53 OSA / NI 45-106 as at Jan 2020

PUBLIC RESPONSE: Building on the issuer-based retail point that keeps coming up, the cleanest purchaser-blind exemption on these facts is the cooperative credit association / caisse populaire membership exemption that is being illustrated by E.

That is exactly why the zero-dollar net assets and unemployed offeree is pleaded: the financial condition of the member is immaterial to the exemption.

The New Brunswick domicile does not defeat the Ontario exemption. NI 45-106 is a national instrument and the OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 cooperative exemption is available in Ontario for a distribution of a cooperative credit association’s membership securities to its members, even where the issuer is extra-provincial. The provincial-registration / members-only pleading tension that colleagues have flagged is a drafting nuance, not a bar to the classic members-only reading, and in practice the exemption is relied on precisely for this type of broad retail membership subscription.

That makes E the parallel purchaser-blind retail exemption to the bank-debt point. In contrast A, while the textbook illustration, carries the Schedule II foreign-bank nuance that has been repeatedly debated in this thread. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II bank authorised under the Bank Act, and the bank-debt exemption in NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73 is routinely discussed in the literature as applying to debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act. The Schedule II foreign-ownership / authorisation point is the source of the continuing debate about scope for a retail bond raise by a foreign-bank subsidiary, and it is the reason A is still being qualified as “unambiguous only on a pure debt reading”.

B is not rescued by the bank-debt rationale: JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent, not a Bank Act bank, and no accredited investor, $150k minimum amount or OM eligible investor basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. C fails on accredited / OM eligible investor thresholds: salary $35k and net assets $10k with no connection to the issuer is well below NI 45-106 s.2.3 and the Ontario OM eligible investor thresholds in force in Jan 2020, and no $150k minimum amount is shown. D remains the equity trap: Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the securities are shares. The statutory bank exemption is a debt-securities exemption; a public share offering to retail, including a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser, cannot rely on the bank-debt exemption and no investor-based exemption is made out.

On that reading the textbook purchaser-blind retail compliance is the cooperative credit association member share distribution in E, with the bank debt illustration in A remaining subject to the Schedule II / authorised foreign bank debate. * C. Private issuer to an unconnected purchaser. Co-operative credit association

OSA s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 Part 5 gives an issuer based members-only exemption for the distribution of membership/securities of a co-operative credit association/caisses populaires/credit union to its members. The exemption is not conditioned on net worth/income.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires/co-operative credit association. On the classic members-only teaching the membership share raise is prospectus exempt irrespective of member net assets/income, so a $0 net asset unemployed member is immaterial. That is the textbook parallel to the bank-debt exemption in A.

The factual tension noted in the previous round is the pleading: the distribution is described as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation, and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled. On a strict pleading reading the members-only condition is not made out and the $0 net asset/unemployed offeree would be fatal to an accredited/eligible reliance. On the conventional exam formulation E is the textbook co-operative/credit union member exemption and is therefore compliant; on a strictly pleaded public retail raise to non-members the exemption is not made out.

On that basis the unambiguously, unqualified compliant distribution on the facts stated is A, the Canadian bank debt distribution of Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail investors under the bank-debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated. E is the second issuer-based textbook exemption under the co-operative credit association member exemption, subject to the members-only/provincial pleading caveat above. * Private issuer – investor based

I'm still working from the issuer-based retail exemptions in OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 and NI 45-106 as they stood in Jan 2020, and I think the discussion is really about which of those issuer exemptions is being tested cleanly on the facts.

The Bank Act debt point is real and it's why A keeps surfacing. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and bonds are debt securities. The s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank/financial-institution debt exemption is issuer and security based and purchaser blind. On a pure debt reading that exemption is engaged.

That is also why the bank example is less clean in this set than it first looks. The exemption is debt only, which is why the Fairstone Bank of Canada shares in D are routinely used as the trap: bank equity is not bank debt, and no accredited/OM/$150k basis is pleaded for a $0 net asset unemployed offeree. The Schedule II foreign-ownership point for Bank of China Canada is the point that is normally used to generate debate about scope in a retail bond raise, and the debt-only limitation that makes D non-compliant makes the bank-debt illustration feel contingent.

The purchaser-blind retail illustration that is actually purchaser blind in the textbook sense is the cooperative credit association / caisse populaire membership exemption. OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 Part 5 provide a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / credit union / caisse populaire to its members. It is issuer/member based and it is expressly not conditioned on net worth, income, accredited or eligible investor status.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires / co-operative credit association. The fact pattern is the classic exam fact: a members share subscription by a caisse populaire aimed at a broad retail membership base, including a member with $0 net assets who is unemployed. That zero-asset/unemployed member is not a defect; it is the point of the exemption. The exemption does not require a financial test of the member and it does not care about employment.

B is not rescued by the bank debt analysis. The Canadian bank debt exemption is for debt of a Bank Act bank authorised in Canada. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the US parent and no accredited, $150k minimum amount or OM basis is made out for a large number of Canadian investors. C is a private issuer to an unconnected person with salary $35k and net assets $10k, well below the Jan 2020 accredited and OM eligible investor thresholds and no $150k minimum amount or family/friends connection.

On the conventional teaching the unambiguous retail-compliant issuer-based examples are the bank debt exemption and its parallel, the cooperative credit-union membership exemption. In this set E is that parallel and, on the pleaded facts, is the cleaner purchaser-blind retail illustration: a co-operative credit association membership share raise where the financial condition of the member is immaterial.

I think we are all on the same structure now and the elimination is clear.

* C is dead on arrival. Private issuer to an unconnected person with $35k salary and $10k net assets is nowhere near accredited investor s.2.3, nor OM eligible investor thresholds in Ontario Jan 2020, and there is no $150k minimum amount or family/friends basis.
* B is not rescued by the bank-debt exemption. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent, not a Bank Act bank, and no accredited/minimum amount/OM basis is made out for a large retail Canadian raise.
* D is the equity trap. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The statutory bank/financial institution exemption we rely on for bank debt is a debt-securities exemption. A public retail share offering by a bank that expressly includes a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser cannot be made on an accredited/eligible/minimum amount basis, so D is prospectus required on the conventional debt-only reading.

That leaves A and E as the two issuer-based retail exemptions.

A, Bank of China Canada bonds to retail, is the textbook bank-debt illustration and the group is right that s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is issuer and security based and purchaser blind. The residual nuance that keeps coming up is the Schedule II foreign-bank point. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II foreign bank authorised in Canada and the literature is not uniform on how the “bank constituted under the Bank Act” language is applied to Schedule II debt marketed broadly to Ontario retail. That is why the exam uses the bank-debt fact pattern as a teaching point rather than as the cleanest unambiguous call.

E is the purchaser-blind issuer exemption in its purest form. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire. NI 45-106 Part 5 and OSA s.73 provide a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership/securities of a co-operative credit association to its members. The exemption is issuer/member based and is expressly not conditioned on net worth, income or employment.

That is exactly why the fact pattern gives us a member with zero dollars of net assets who is unemployed. That is not a defect for the exemption, it is the point of the exemption. The members-only co-operative exemption is built to allow a retail membership share raise by a caisse populaire to its members without accredited/eligible investor testing. The “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” wording is the normal way the members share subscription is pleaded in an exam.

Read as the textbook members-only co-operative credit union raise, E is the unambiguously compliant distribution and it is the parallel issuer-based illustration to the bank-debt point in A. If I have to pick the single most exam-like compliant example on the facts as drafted, it is the co-operative membership share raise in E, with A being the familiar bank-debt companion example.

Ontario Jan 2020 s.53 OSA / NI 45-106 / Rule 45-501

The prospectus requirement is displaced for a retail raise only by the issuer based
financial-institution exemptions and by the investor based accredited / OM / minimum
amount / family friends exemptions.

Bank / financial institution debt

NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73.1 is a blanket issuer and security based exemption for a
distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or
insurance company constituted under an Act of the Parliament of Canada. It is
purchaser blind and it is debt only.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities
of that Canadian Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its own debt to the
retail public is the classic s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank-debt exemption. The retail
character of the offerees is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario.

* B. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent / non-Bank Act issuer. The
Canadian bank-debt exemption is limited to debt of a bank constituted under the Bank
Act of Canada / an authorised Canadian Schedule II bank, and no accredited investor,
OM eligible investor, $150k minimum amount s.2.10 or family/friends/business
associate basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. B is prospectus
required.

Private issuer / investor based

* C. Private issuer to an unconnected individual. Jan 2020 accredited is net
financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k / $300k with spouse in each
of the two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible is ≈ net assets $400k or net income
$75k in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35k and net assets $10k, no
connection and no $150k minimum amount. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption
is made out. C is non-compliant.

Bank equity vs bank debt

The statutory bank exemption is a debt securities exemption.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares.
A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail investors, and in
particular to a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by
the bank-debt exemption and no accredited / OM / minimum amount basis is made out
on the facts. On the prevailing debt-only reading of s.73/NI 45-106 D is prospectus
required.

Co-operative credit association

OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 Part 5 gives an issuer based members-only exemption for the
distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / caisses
populaires / credit union to its members. The exemption is not conditioned on net
worth or income.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires / co-operative credit
association. On the textbook members-only reading the membership share issue is
prospectus exempt irrespective of the member’s financial condition, so a $0 net
asset unemployed member would be immaterial. The facts as pleaded however describe
the raise as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with
no express members-only pleading, and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled. On a
strict pleading reading the members-only condition is not made out and the
distribution would be prospectus required on the basis of the zero-asset unemployed
offeree.

On the facts as stated the unambiguously compliant, purchaser blind retail
distribution is A, the non-prospectus distribution of bonds by Bank of China Canada.
B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated, with E being textbook compliant
only on a true members-only reading which is not expressly pleaded here.
